opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that a lot of the work we did at Google, and that many other groups did over the past decade, was really about figuring out the individual ingredients. We learned a lot about how to do large-scale data collection with real robots. Some of the early arm farm work, for example, where we had a bunch of robots grasping objects for months on end, showed that if you just collect enough real-world experience, you can get surprisingly robust behaviors. Then things like QT-Opt showed you could do reinforcement learning at scale on real hardware. And later, the RT-1 and RT-2 line of work showed that you could take large transformer-based models, and even vision-language models pre-trained on web data, and turn them into robot policies that inherit some of that semantic knowledge.

But each of those was, in a sense, a proof of concept for one piece of the puzzle. The challenge now is putting the pieces together into something that actually behaves like a foundation model, meaning something that's general enough that you can take it, give it a new robot or a new task, and with relatively little additional effort, get it to do something useful.

And I think there are a few things that make that hard. One is data diversity. In language, the internet just hands you an enormous, incredibly diverse dataset. In robotics there's no equivalent, so you have to think hard about how to combine data from many different robots, many different environments, many different tasks. Efforts like Open X-Embodiment were really an early step toward saying, okay, maybe the data from a robot in one lab and a robot in another lab can actually help each other, even if the hardware is different.

The second thing is the gap between understanding and acting. Vision-language models know a lot about the world, but knowing what a cup is and knowing how to physically pick it up with the right force, at the right angle, while it's sliding on the table, are very different kinds of knowledge. So a big part of the challenge is figuring out architectures and training recipes that preserve that rich semantic knowledge while adding really dexterous, high-frequency physical control on top of it.

And the third is that, ultimately, I think these systems have to get better through their own experience. Imitation from demonstrations gets you a long way, but if you want robots that are really reliable, that recover from mistakes, that get faster and more robust over time, you need them to learn from what they do in the real world. So the question is how to close that loop at scale.

So I'd say the past research gave us confidence that each of these is possible. What we're trying to do now is build the full system where all of these things work together, and where the model gets more capable as you put more data and more robots into it, much like we've seen with language models.

r001.rationale: The response describes combining research ingredients into a full system and scaling data and robots, but does not state that an industrial-scale building effort beyond fundamental research is required.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the technical challenge of integrating capabilities, but does not identify a singular organizational focus on making robotic foundation models work as an end in itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth starting with what we actually learned from that period, because a lot of the work we did at Google, and before that at Berkeley, was really about one question: can you get robots to learn from large amounts of their own experience, the way the rest of machine learning was learning from large amounts of data? And the honest answer at the time was, sort of. We could show that it worked in principle. We had the arm farm, we had RT-1, RT-2, these systems where you collect a lot of robot data and you train one big policy on it. And the exciting thing was that the recipe kept pointing in the same direction as the rest of AI. More data, bigger models, better. That part transferred.

What didn't transfer cleanly is the data itself. In language, the internet had already done the hard work for you. Somebody had written down a huge fraction of what humans know how to say. For robots there's nothing like that. There's no internet of robot experience. So every one of those projects ended up being, in large part, a data collection project disguised as a modeling project. And you learn pretty quickly that the modeling part is almost the easy part now. The thing that determines whether a robotic foundation model works is whether you've figured out how to get enough of the right kind of experience into it, and whether you've structured the training so that the model can actually absorb diversity rather than just memorize the one lab setup it was trained in.

So when I think about building on that work, I think about a few things we got right and a few we got wrong. What we got right is the commitment to end to end learning, to not hand-designing the perception pipeline or the planner, because every time you insert hand-engineering you're inserting a ceiling. What we got wrong, or at least underestimated, is how much the research framing itself constrained things. In a research lab you want a clean result. You want to say, here's the method, here's the ablation, it beats the baseline. And that pushes you toward narrow, controlled settings. But the whole point of a foundation model is that it has to work out of the narrow setting. It has to work in somebody's kitchen that you've never seen. You can't ablate your way to that.

The other thing I'd say, and this is really why Physical Intelligence exists, is that there's a kind of work that's very hard to do inside a large company or a university, which is the unglamorous engineering of actually operationalizing the data flywheel. Getting robots deployed, having them do real tasks, having that experience come back and improve the model, and doing that at a scale where the model actually gets better rather than just the paper getting written. That's not a research contribution in the traditional sense, but it's the thing that makes the whole approach real. I think the lesson from the Google era is that we proved the thesis, and now the challenge is much less about proving it and much more about building the machine that lets the thesis play out.

And I'd add one more thing. People sometimes talk about pre-training on internet video or on language models as a shortcut around the data problem, and I think that's half right. Those models give you a lot of semantic understanding of the world for free, and that matters. But understanding what a cup is and understanding how it feels to grasp a cup when it's slightly wet are different things, and the second one you only get from the robot actually doing it. So the way I see it, the past research gave us the architecture of the solution. What's left is the part where you actually have to touch the world a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says robotic foundation models need the large-scale engineering of deploying robots, collecting real-task experience, and feeding it back into models; it calls this work what makes the approach real.

r002.rationale: The response says this work is why Physical Intelligence exists, but does not clearly state that a singular organizational focus on making the models work as an end in itself is necessary.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is that there’s a lot you can build on in terms of methods and experience, but much less you can take for granted in terms of infrastructure and data. A robotics project might produce a very impressive result, but that result depends on a particular robot, a particular setup, and a particular collection of tasks. The next project changes some of those things, and suddenly it’s difficult to reuse what you learned.

For a robotic foundation model, you want that relationship to be different. You want every additional task, every additional environment, ideally every additional robot, to contribute to a system that gets better overall. Making that happen is partly a question of model design, but it’s also a question of how you collect data and how you represent actions across different embodiments.

And there’s a practical difficulty here: the data you collect depends on what your robot can already do. If it can’t accomplish anything useful, you have to provide demonstrations or otherwise guide it. As it becomes more capable, it can potentially collect more of its own experience. So you’re trying to get that process started and make sure that improvements in capability actually translate into better learning.

I’d frame the goal as making the research cumulative. Can a new task build on everything the system has learned before, and then contribute something back? That’s a much more demanding standard than showing that a robot can perform one task very well.

r001.rationale: The response discusses infrastructure, data, and cumulative research, but does not state that success requires an industrial-scale building effort beyond fundamental research.

r002.rationale: The response describes making research cumulative, but does not identify a singular organizational focus on making robotic foundation models work as an end in itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is figuring out which parts of that work become more useful as you scale, and which parts were really solutions to the constraints of a particular experiment.

In robotics, you can get a very impressive result by carefully designing the task, the environment, and the data collection process. But then it’s hard to tell how much of the capability is in the learned model and how much is in everything you built around it. If you want a foundation model, you need that capability to carry over when the environment changes, when the robot changes, or when somebody asks it to do something you didn’t anticipate.

So I wouldn’t think of the goal as simply taking a successful robotics system and making the neural network bigger. You have to build a learning process where additional experience reliably improves generalization. That means thinking about the data, the training objective, and how the robot can collect useful experience after deployment.

And there’s a kind of chicken-and-egg problem here: you need a reasonably capable robot to collect diverse, useful data, but you need that data to build a capable robot. The way forward is probably an iterative process. You start with the capabilities and data you have, use those to make collecting the next round of experience easier, and keep expanding what the system can do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling, data collection, and iterative learning, but does not state that an industrial-scale building effort beyond fundamental research is required.

r002.rationale: The response describes an iterative path forward, but does not identify a singular organizational focus on making robotic foundation models work as an end in itself.
